quiz.question: Which register identifies the current instruction stream on x86-64?
options: RSP
RIP
CR3
RFLAGS
quiz.explanation: On x86-64, the Instruction Pointer (RIP) holds the 64-bit virtual address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed by the CPU. (On AArch64, the equivalent register is PC). RSP is the stack pointer, CR3 points to the page table root, and RFLAGS stores CPU condition codes.

quiz.question: Why does an ordinary application use a system call to request protected kernel services?
options: The CPU cannot execute arithmetic in user mode
Hardware privilege mechanisms restrict direct privileged operations
Every function call enters the kernel
System calls automatically create new processes
quiz.explanation: Processors enforce hardware privilege rings (Ring 3 vs Ring 0). Unprivileged user-mode code is prohibited from executing privileged CPU instructions (such as disabling interrupts or modifying page tables) or accessing physical device controllers directly. System calls provide a hardware-gated interface to request supervisor services.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a context switch from a mode switch?
options: A context switch changes the executing thread; a mode switch changes privilege level
They are always identical
A mode switch always changes the physical CPU
A context switch only occurs during boot
quiz.explanation: A mode switch transitions the current CPU between privilege states (e.g. Ring 3 user mode to Ring 0 kernel mode for a syscall) while continuing the exact same thread of execution. A context switch saves the architectural state of one thread and restores that of another, switching which task is running.

quiz.question: Which statement about page faults is correct?
options: Every page fault means invalid memory access
Every page fault reads data from an SSD
Some page faults are handled successfully by the OS
A page fault is the same as a TLB miss
quiz.explanation: Page faults are a standard mechanism of virtual memory. Many page faults are completely routine and resolved successfully by the kernel, such as demand paging (allocating zeroed physical pages on first touch) and copy-on-write (COW) page duplication during fork().

quiz.question: What does DMA primarily allow?
options: A CPU to skip all device management
A device or controller to transfer data to or from memory without CPU copying every byte
An application to bypass memory protection
An SSD to replace RAM
quiz.explanation: Direct Memory Access (DMA) enables high-speed peripheral controllers (such as NVMe SSDs, 100GbE NICs, and GPUs) to transfer data directly into or out of system DRAM over the PCIe bus without requiring the CPU to execute programmed I/O loops copying every byte.

quiz.question: Which component commonly loads the Linux kernel during a PC boot?
options: The CPU cache
A bootloader such as GRUB
The shell
The application linker
quiz.explanation: On PC systems, after UEFI or BIOS firmware initializes fundamental hardware, it invokes a bootloader such as GRUB (or systemd-boot). The bootloader loads the compressed Linux kernel image (vmlinuz) and initial ramdisk (initramfs) into memory and transfers control to the kernel entry point.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a TLB?
options: Store the entire operating system
Cache address translations to reduce translation overhead
Store all persistent files
Schedule CPU threads
quiz.explanation: The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is an on-chip associative cache inside the MMU that stores recent virtual-to-physical address mappings. A TLB hit resolves an address translation in ~1 clock cycle, avoiding costly 4-level or 5-level page table memory walks.

quiz.question: What does a hardware timer help an OS achieve?
options: Permanent CPU ownership by one process
Preemptive scheduling and time-related operations
Automatic compilation of every program
Elimination of device interrupts
quiz.explanation: A programmable hardware timer (such as the APIC timer or HPET) periodically sends hardware interrupts to the CPU. This allows the operating system kernel to regain control from CPU-bound tasks, update time slices, and enforce preemptive multitasking.
